storm.summary_layperson: A cluster of showers and storms is parked about 35 miles north over the Hudson Valley, and it's barely moving toward us, so the near-term threat here stays modest tonight.
storm.local_effect_blurb: The Sound's marine layer holds a healthy 9°F air–water gap right now (fading to about 3°F by 8 PM), but this storm's track is staying inland to the north instead of crossing the Sound, so that usual buffer isn't a factor tonight.
storm.detail_html:
Radar (KOKX, scanned 8:24 PM) shows a cluster of showers and thunderstorms centered about 35–38 miles north of the cove, over the lower Hudson Valley, with peak reflectivity of 44 dBZ. The cell is essentially stationary relative to the cove — measured closing speed is a mere 0.7 kt — so this reads as a moderate-risk night (a ≥35 dBZ cell within 50 miles) rather than an imminent threat.

Instability is thin: CAPE sits at just 150 J/kg per the latest HRRR run, well under the 1,500 J/kg level that would flag a punch-through risk, even though deep-layer shear is unusually strong at 55–65 kt. That combination — strong shear, weak fuel — tends to produce organized but modest convection rather than explosive updrafts, matching the NWS forecast discussion's own read that the severe threat is low and any stronger cells are more likely well south of us.

The Sound's usual buffer isn't deciding tonight's outcome. Water is running 75°F against 84°F air — a 9°F gap that would normally support a moderate marine stable layer capable of choking incoming cells. But this approach is from due north, essentially parallel to the coast, so the storm never has to cross the cool water before it could reach the cove. That's why the local effect reads neutral rather than mitigating — the mechanism exists, it's just not the one in play for this track.

For context on how that buffer is trending anyway, in case something later tracks across the Sound instead: the 9°F gap holds through about 6 PM, narrows to roughly 6°F by 7 PM, and drops under the 5°F protective threshold by 7:24 PM as the air cools faster than the water. By 9 PM the gap goes negative — water warmer than air — so anything crossing the Sound after full dark gets no cooling assist at all.

Bottom line for the cove versus surrounding towns: with instability this low and the cell essentially parked to the north, Riverside's outlook isn't meaningfully different from Stamford, Rye, or White Plains tonight. What would change the call: the cell actually starting to close on the cove (currently near-zero motion), CAPE climbing toward the 1,500–3,000 J/kg range as the evening destabilizes further, or a track shift that sends new development across the Sound instead of staying inland.

wind.tactics_blurb: Pure sea-breeze evening out of the SSE, mature and oscillating through about 7 PM — play the shifts rather than banging a corner. Pressure favors the west shore (Belle Haven/Indian Harbor), the right side of the beat looking upwind, since Tod's Point shelters the east side in this direction. The thermal collapses hard around 7:23 PM, 30 minutes before the 7:53 PM sunset, so a start after roughly 7:15 PM is racing on borrowed time.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
This is a pure thermal sea-breeze day (not reinforced) — the two-ingredient test is satisfied on the thermal side (9.4°F air–water differential, well above the 5°F gate) but the background gradient is light and offshore: the NWS forecast has today's synoptic wind at NE around 3 mph, essentially calm and not adding to the sea breeze. That combination puts today squarely in the pure-thermal regime rather than the reinforced sub-case.

HRRR is running behind the real sea breeze on direction, as it typically does on western-LIS thermal days: the model's near-term surface wind reads SE (141°) while Riverside YC and the western-LIS station cluster are already reading SSW (194°), a 53° divergence. Applying the maturation correction pulls the forecast direction to SSE (156°) for the next couple of hours — expect the wind to sit and oscillate in the SSE–SSW band through peak sea breeze, roughly ±15° each side of the mean, since the breeze has been running long enough to be fully mature rather than still ramping.

Pressure in the cove: with flow out of the SSE, Greenwich Point (Tod's Point) partially shelters the east side of the course, so the west shore — Belle Haven / Indian Harbor — carries more consistent pressure. Looking upwind (south) from the start, that's the right-hand side of the beat.

The thermal collapses on schedule: the sea breeze needs the 5°F+ air–water gap to keep running, and that gap crosses below threshold at 7:24 PM, thirty minutes ahead of the 7:53 PM sunset. Expect speed to fall off hard through the 7 PM hour and bottom out light-and-variable by 8 PM.

What happens after the collapse is lower-confidence: HRRR's raw output (no longer correction-eligible once the thermal is gone) shows a light NE flow filling back in around 9–10 PM, 7–10 kt. That's model-only guidance this far out and it lines up with the stalled storm cluster sitting about 35 miles north — treat it as background gradient, not a repeat of the sea breeze, and don't count on it for racing.

data_caveats: Storm cell motion discarded as a centroid-displacement artifact (implied 82 kt); arrival timing falls back to HRRR-steering estimate only, no confirmed ETA for the parked northern cell.
